Iran has survived decades of sanctions. Faced with more, it is likely to escalate rather than surrender, analysts said.

# Iranian lawmaker says Tehran would respond in kind if US used nuclear weapon

National Security and Foreign Policy Commission member comments on media claim about possibility of US nuclear attack on Iran

Sahin Demir

19 August 2026•Update: 19 August 2026

![Content media](https://web-cdnprod.aa.com.tr/uploads/Contents/2026/08/19/thumbs_b_c_786ccd648e7d96fb5a061bb702e0f40f.jpg)

ISTANBUL

An Iranian lawmaker said Tehran would respond in kind if the US used a nuclear weapon against Iran, commenting on a media report about the possibility of such an attack, according to local media on Wednesday.

Fada Hossein Maleki, a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, made the remarks in an interview with Iranian news outlet Khabar Online.

Asked how likely he considered a US nuclear attack on Iran, Maleki said: “I do not rule out an ill-considered action by (US President Donald) Trump, but I do not think he would dare to do such a thing, because such an action could plunge the world into a dangerous war.”

“If such an action is taken, the Islamic Republic of Iran will also respond, and its reaction will be proportionate to the type of weapon used against Iran,” he added.

### The New "Phony War" in the Middle East

The American-Iranian War has entered a quiet yet tense phase reminiscent of Western Europe's "Phony War" in early 1940. While large-scale combat operations have slowed, key strategic shifts are taking place across Washington, Tehran, and Middle Eastern capitals.  
 In this episode of Jerusalem Studio, our panel breaks down President Trump’s evolving priorities focusing heavily on reopening the Strait of Hormuz to lower domestic US fuel prices and containing Iran’s nuclear ambitions, while shifting focus away from regime collapse, ballistic missile dismantling, and severing Tehran’s proxy networks.  
 00:00 - Introduction: The US-Iran "Phony War" Phase  
 00:42 - Shift in Trump’s Priorities: Hormuz & Fuel Prices vs. Nuclear Ambitions  
 01:19 - Is Israel Left Alone Against Regional Proxies?

"The president is playing the long game," said the energy secretary.

![](https://i.abcnewsfe.com/a/728b0596-ba8d-4a02-9446-8e32c41c4545/donald-trump-13-rt-gmh-260817_1786990751275_hpMain_16x9.jpg?w=992)

The Trump administration appears to be indicating it favors economic warfare in its approach to the conflict with Iran, touting its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and previewing new sanctions still to be announced.

President Donald Trump, who has often discussed tight deadlines for diplomacy with Iran, has suggested the U.S. might attempt a longer-term squeeze, telling Fox News in an interview on Monday he is "not in a hurry" to bring about a solution.

A 60-day memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran to lay the groundwork for an end to the war has expired and there is no other agreement to replace it.

The effects of the blockade, intended to deny any Iranian exports through the strait, could take months to bear effects on the Iranian economy, experts said, and it is not clear whether pressure from the blockade or any new actions could change Tehran's position at a future negotiating table.

# Six Months Into the Iran War: The Search for an Endgame

Six months into the US-Iran war, both sides remain locked in a strategic deadlock. Iran seeks to exploit energy-market risks, US military costs and regional vulnerabilities, while Washington is likely to sustain economic pressure, coercive strikes and pursue a limited agreement.

![](/sites/default/files/articles/2026-08/web%20%284%29_0.jpg)

Screen capture of an IRGC video showing the deployment and launch of a ballistic missile. [IRGC]

## Introduction

As the direct military confrontation between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the United States enters its sixth month, questions are mounting over how the conflict might ultimately end. With neither side appearing willing to retreat and both moving toward a complete deadlock, several broad strategic trajectories can be identified that may shape the conflict’s course. The precise contours of what lies ahead, however, remain uncertain.
